statement: In people who smoked and joined trials of nicotine replacement for stopping smoking, chest pain or palpitations were reported more often with nicotine replacement than with placebo or no replacement: 2.5% against 1.4% (about 1 more in 100; odds ratio 1.88, 95% CI 1.37 to 2.57; the 15 trials that reported them, 11,074 people, including trials outside the review's main analysis; Cochrane review, search to July 2017). That review did not pool other side effects, because the trials reported them too differently, and lists them by form: with gum, hiccups, stomach upset, jaw pain and tooth or mouth problems; with the patch, skin irritation (up to 54% of people in one source it cites, usually mild); with the inhaler and sprays, irritation of the mouth, throat or nose, cough and runny nose; with sublingual tablets, hiccups, mouth burning, sore throat, cough, dry lips and mouth ulcers. Serious events were not pooled against placebo or no replacement: a patch trial in people with cardiovascular disease and six trials in pregnancy did not detect more serious events with nicotine replacement. In a later review comparing ways of using nicotine replacement (68 trials; search to April 2022), serious events were too few to compare (combination against a single form: 3 against 1 in 1,000, interval 1 to 18, seven events in total; risk ratio 4.44, 0.76 to 25.85; 5 trials, 2,888 people; low certainty), and more people stopped treatment because of side effects with fast-acting forms than with the patch (23 against 5 in 1,000; risk ratio 4.23, 1.54 to 11.63; 3 trials, 1,482 people; very low certainty), including 3.0% with a nasal spray against 0.9% with the patch in one trial of 922 people. All of this comes from treatment lasting weeks to months in people motivated to quit, so it cannot show how often rare serious events happen or what longer use does. Certainty: low (for the chest pain or palpitations result; the later review's figures carry its own lower ratings, and the lists of local effects are not graded). Status: mixed.
plain: In trials of nicotine replacement for stopping smoking, side effects were mostly local, depending on the form: skin irritation with patches, and effects in the mouth, throat or nose with gum, lozenges, sprays and inhalers. Chest pain or palpitations were reported by about 2.5 in 100 people given nicotine replacement and about 1.4 in 100 given a dummy product or nothing. Serious health events were too few and too unevenly reported to say whether nicotine replacement changes them. More people stopped treatment because of side effects with fast-acting forms than with the patch (about 23 in 1,000 against 5 in 1,000). All of this comes from weeks to months of use.
population: People who smoked and joined trials of nicotine replacement for stopping smoking (136 studies in the 2018 review, chest pain or palpitations reported in 15 trials with 11,074 people; 68 trials in the 2023 review, serious events reported in 5 combination trials with 2,888 people), treated for weeks to months
exposure: Nicotine replacement in any form (gum, patch, lozenge or tablet, inhaler, nasal or oral spray), alone or combined
comparator: Placebo or no nicotine replacement; a single form of nicotine replacement; the nicotine patch (for fast-acting forms)
outcome: Chest pain or palpitations; local side effects by form; serious adverse events; withdrawal from treatment because of side effects, as reported in the trials
magnitude: Chest pain or palpitations: OR 1.88 (95% CI 1.37–2.57), 15 trials, 11,074 participants; 2.5% with NRT vs 1.4% with control (about 1 more in 100, editors' subtraction). An earlier meta-analysis cited by the review (12 studies) gave OR 2.06 (1.51–2.82) and overlaps these trials. Serious adverse events, combination vs single form: RR 4.44 (0.76–25.85), 5 trials, 2,888 participants; 1 vs 3 per 1,000 (1–18); seven events in total; low certainty. Withdrawals due to treatment: combination vs single form RR 1.12 (0.57–2.20; 5 trials; 3,070; I² 73%; 12 vs 14 per 1,000; very low); fast-acting form vs patch RR 4.23 (1.54–11.63; 3 trials; 1,482; 5 vs 23 per 1,000, 8–63; very low); nasal spray vs patch RR 3.47 (1.15–10.46; 1 trial; 922; 3.0% vs 0.9%). Serious events, fast-acting form vs patch: 3 of 4 trials (1,252 participants) had none; the fourth RR 1.75 (0.52–5.92; 642); very low certainty.

evidence.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Adverse events, 3rd paragraph; Data and analyses, Comparison 6
evidence.extracted: Chest pain or palpitations: odds ratio 1.88 (1.37 to 2.57), 15 included and excluded trials in which they were reported, 11,074 participants, with 2.5% of NRT groups and 1.4% of control groups affected (editors' subtraction: about 1 more in 100). An earlier meta-analysis (Mills 2010) found OR 2.06 (1.51 to 2.82) in 12 studies. The authors call the events extremely rare and report no evidence of an excess of serious cardiac problems.

evidence.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Adverse events, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Appendix 3
evidence.extracted: Adverse events were not pooled, because the nature, timing and duration of symptoms were reported too variably; they are tabulated by trial in Appendix 3. Local effects listed: gum, hiccups, gastrointestinal disturbance, jaw pain, orodental problems; patch, skin sensitivity and irritation (up to 54% of people in one cited source, usually mild); inhalator and nasal and oral sprays, irritation at the site of use (throat irritation, coughing, oral burning; nasal irritation and runny nose; hiccups); sublingual tablets, hiccups, burning in the mouth, sore throat, cough, dry lips, mouth ulcers. Adolescents reported similar events to adults.

evidence.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Adverse events, 3rd, 4th and 5th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: In one patch trial in people with cardiovascular disease (Joseph 1996) there was no evidence that serious adverse events were more common with the patch, and cardiovascular events such as worse angina (about 16% of participants) did not differ by arm. Six trials in pregnant women did not detect significant increases in serious adverse events. A network meta-analysis the review cites (Mills 2014) found more cardiovascular events with NRT than with placebo overall, driven by lower-level events; its figures are quoted from another review and were not checked.

evidence.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Combination therapy › Combination versus single form, 3rd to 5th paragraphs; Summary of findings, Table 1; Appendix 2
evidence.extracted: Combination against single form: serious adverse events RR 4.44 (0.76 to 25.85), 5 studies, 2,888 participants, seven events in total, 1 per 1,000 with a single form against 3 per 1,000 (1 to 18) with combination, low certainty (two levels for imprecision); any cardiac event RR 0.66 (0.22 to 2.05; 2 studies; 656); withdrawals due to treatment RR 1.12 (0.57 to 2.20; 5 studies; 3,070; I² 73%), 12 per 1,000 with a single form against 14 with combination, very low certainty. Only 3 of the 16 combination trials reported cardiac events; Piper 2009 (1,504 participants) reported 32 serious events not split by arm.

evidence.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Fast-acting NRT versus patch, 2nd to 4th paragraphs; Summary of findings, Table 5
evidence.extracted: Fast-acting forms against the patch: withdrawals due to treatment RR 4.23 (1.54 to 11.63), 3 studies, 1,482 participants, 5 per 1,000 with the patch against 23 per 1,000 (8 to 63) with fast-acting forms, very low certainty; nasal spray against patch RR 3.47 (1.15 to 10.46), 1 study, 922, 3.0% against 0.9%. Serious events: three of four studies had none (1,252 participants in all four); the fourth RR 1.75 (0.52 to 5.92; 642 participants); very low certainty. Cardiac events reported by arm in one small trial: none in either arm.

evidence.locator: Discussion › Overall completeness and applicability of evidence, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Authors' conclusions › Implications for practice
evidence.extracted: The authors state that evidence for the safety and tolerability of different ways of using NRT is limited, that many comparisons rest on sparse studies and that further research could strengthen or change the findings.

risk_of_bias.note: Side effects defined and collected differently across trials; only 15 of 136 trials reported chest pain or palpitations; many trials unblinded.

imprecision.note: About 200 events in the chest pain or palpitations pool (editors' estimate); serious events seven in total (the 2023 review: two levels).

grade.reasoning: Randomised evidence, starting high; the rating is for the main finding, chest pain or palpitations, and the other figures in the statement are labelled with the lower ratings the 2023 review gave them. Risk of bias, one level: side effects were not defined, timed or collected in a common way (the 2018 review did not pool them because of extensive variation in reporting), the chest pain or palpitations result comes from the 15 trials that reported them out of 136, 43 trials had no matched placebo, and in the 2023 review two of the four or three trials behind the serious-event and withdrawal rows were at high risk of bias. Imprecision, one level: by the editors' arithmetic from the percentages, assuming equal group sizes, the chest pain or palpitations result has about 200 events, fewer than the 300 usually wanted, and serious events were so few (seven in the combination comparison) that the 2023 review took two levels. Inconsistency, not rated down for the main finding; the withdrawal figure for combination use has I² 73% and is labelled very low. Indirectness, not rated down: the claim is limited to what trials of nicotine replacement for stopping smoking recorded. An earlier meta-analysis of this outcome (12 studies, OR 2.06) overlaps these trials and is not counted as independent replication. Status mixed because most harm outcomes were too variably reported to pool, not because trials disagreed about chest pain or palpitations. The claim does not use figures from the cited network meta-analysis (not checked) or the 2023 review's comparisons of doses and timing, which are on that review's study card.

verification.flag_note: Harms are staged apart from cl_nic_nrt because the evidence is weaker (the 2018 review did not rate or pool them; the 2023 review rated serious events low and withdrawals very low). Relation is-associated-with and status mixed are the editors' cautious reading; the senior author may prefer other labels. Left on the study cards only: higher-dose patch withdrawals and serious events, palpitations with early (pre-quit) use. The 2023 plain language summary says nicotine replacement is safe to use on the strength of the 2018 review; this claim does not repeat that wording, because the 2018 review did not pool serious events and found chest pain or palpitations at 2.5% against 1.4% (see the Theodoulou card). Not read: Appendix 3 and Appendix 2 beyond the text, the cited network meta-analyses.
